title: Frontoparietal Control (Multiple-Demand) Network

html:
The frontoparietal control (FPN; also called "multiple-demand" (MD) or "central executive" (CEN)) network is best understood as a domain-general operating system for cognition: a set of reusable, parameterizable control routines instantiated in lateral PFC and posterior parietal cortex, positioned mid-way along the principal cortical connectivity gradient-between unimodal sensorimotor systems and the transmodal apex occupied by the default-mode network-so they can flexibly couple outward to DAN or inward to DMN as goals dictate 1, 2. Across tasks, these regions are the first to ramp with load and the ones whose whole-brain coupling patterns change the most, supporting rapid instructed task learning and novel rule composition. Recent syntheses argue that cognitive flexibility arises from shifts in "network activity flows" driven by these hubs, rather than from isolated, task-specific modules-a framing that unifies decades of "MD" findings under a single control-flow mechanism 3, 4. A 2025 MEG study decodes cognitive demand across multiple tasks (Figure).

Anatomically, the network’s cortical core spans mid-to-rostral middle frontal gyrus (BA 9/46), inferior frontal gyrus, and dorsomedial premotor/pre-SMA, coupled to intraparietal and inferior parietal sectors. Importantly, it is not content-free: multivariate decoding in 2024 shows robust task and stimulus codes within MD core, with mixed selectivity that scales with difficulty-exactly the representational profile needed to bind abstract rules to concrete inputs and actions 5. Within the frontoparietal complex, there is reliable internal heterogeneity: one subnetwork preferentially aligns with the default-mode system and another with the dorsal attention system, reflecting the FPN’s ability to flexibly interface with networks handling both internal simulation and attention to concrete external stimuli 6.

The parietal arm of the system computes compact, short-horizon affordance maps-the space of immediately available actions over millisecond-second horizons-while prefrontal sectors condition these maps on longer-horizon goals. Work from the "affordance-competition" framework shows parallel representation and selection among potential actions across parietal and premotor fields, with prefrontal and basal ganglia biases resolving the competition as task demands evolve 7, 8; for instance, LIP/IPS may encode saccade-biased spatial priority while AIP codes grasp postures for object shape while prefrontal and basal ganglia biases resolve the competition. This account fits the MD system’s role in moment-to-moment control and clarifies why parietal nodes are so tightly coupled to scene structure and the "now," while prefrontal nodes carry the rule and policy context.

The wiring that makes this possible is specific. SLF II links angular gyrus/IPS to mid-lateral PFC (MFG/dlPFC), SLF III links inferior parietal regions to IFG, and long tracts like the arcuate and IFOF bridge temporal/occipital content stores to prefrontal control 9. These routes concretize how rules in PFC reach parietal affordance maps and, when needed, how stored lexical/semantic or visual knowledge is pulled into the control loop. Diffusion and dissection work in 2022-2025 sharpens these trajectories, and intraoperative stimulation confirms causal contributions of SLF II/III segments to task performance 10, 11.

Subcortically, mediodorsal (MD) thalamus is a peer partner. Closed MD<->PFC loops regulate recurrent PFC dynamics, stabilize task set under uncertainty, and coordinate inter-areal coupling for flexible cognition. A 2024 review and 2025 modeling work converge on a picture where MD adjusts prefrontal gain and uncertainty-dependent gating, complementing basal ganglia loops that gate what is updated 12, 13. This division of labor makes thalamus indispensable for the sustained, context-sensitive stability that complex tasks require.

At the network level, the MD/FPN’s operation is best captured along two coupled axes-spectral composition and intrinsic timescale. As control demands rise, fronto-parietal hubs reliably ramp low-frequency phase coordination, especially midfrontal theta that synchronizes distributed nodes and tracks the need for control across paradigms; large-sample EEG/MEG and reviews in 2024-2025 consolidate this picture, while also noting that scalp theta topographies don’t map one-to-one onto the MD atlas, cautioning against naïve localization 14, 4, 15. Separating periodic from aperiodic signals shows that broadband (aperiodic) power/slope/intercept shifts are the most general neural signature of load, generalizing across tasks and sometimes locking to events 16, 17. Because these aperiodic shifts index aggregate spiking and E-I balance, they provide a task-general, modality-bridging readout of how hard the frontoparietal system is working and when control/learning signals are updating policies. In parallel, intrinsic neural timescales (INT) lengthen in prefrontal cortex as engagement and training increase 18, and recent causal evidence indicates that parietal inputs can selectively dilate prefrontal/FEF timescales 19, providing a concrete mechanism by which task context and long-range biasing tune the integration windows used by control circuitry; population-level fMRI/MEG analyses and modeling converge on plastic, state-dependent timescale gradients spanning cortex 20. Taken together, these results explain both the ubiquity and the burden of MD engagement: the system expands temporal integration to stabilize rules and policy over seconds while coordinating distal regions via slow phase-coupling and broadband upshifts-a powerful, general-purpose control regime that is effective across tasks precisely because it is spectrally and temporally generic.

The cingulo-opercular network (CON)-which recently saw a compelling reframing as the Action-Mode Network (AMN) 21-sets the brain’s global operating context for goal-directed behavior: dACC and anterior insula/fronto-operculum initiate and sustain a high-arousal, externally oriented "action mode" that readies sensorimotor circuits, with the network extending into SMA, aPFC, and supramarginal sectors more broadly than the original CON label implied. In mixed block/event designs, these hubs show the classic start-cue transient followed by block-sustained set activity, consistent with a role in establishing and maintaining the task context across many seconds, while the frontoparietal control network flexibly reconfigures within that context at the trial scale 22, 23. Converging invasive electrophysiology and modeling indicate that anterior insula exerts directed influence over frontoparietal and default-mode systems at control transitions-functioning as a switching hub that helps allocate resources between externally and internally focused modes 24, 25. The AMN’s tonic control is tightly coupled to arousal apparatus: pre-stimulus CON/AMN activity predicts faster responses and sustained alertness, and dACC/insula interact with noradrenergic (LC-NE) and thalamic (including intralaminar) nodes that stabilize the action mode and set overall gain 26, 27. Functionally, cingulo-opercular subnetworks can motivate or "energize" frontoparietal implementations under ambiguity or effort, with late CO signals carrying performance-monitoring and adjustment information that feeds back to FPN to update control policies 28, 29. Pharmacology reinforces the mechanism: α2A-adrenergic stimulation enhances error-based updating in ACC/dlPFC circuits, linking neuromodulatory state to the quality of the action mode 30. In short, the AMN runs upstream in time and upstream in state: it establishes and sustains the arousal-aligned task set and arbitrates large-scale network switching, while the frontoparietal hubs perform rapid, within-mode recombination of rules and adjustments-resolving "who does what" in control and explaining why dACC/insula show onset transients plus block-sustained activity even as FPN keeps reshaping within trials.

Interactions among control and non-control networks are goal-contingent, not hard-wired. During externally focused, high-demand tasks the frontoparietal/MD system rises while the default-mode network (DMN) is actively suppressed, a canonical pattern linked to better control performance; when the problem benefits from internal simulation-autobiographical planning, hypothesis generation, creative search-frontoparietal and DMN co-activate and couple, and time-resolved analyses show that the capacity to dynamically switch between these systems predicts divergent-thinking ability at scale (with evidence for an inverted-U dependence on switching), rather than a simple monotonic anti-correlation 31, 32, 33. Within frontoparietal cortex this flexibility is scaffolded by heterogeneity: one subnetwork aligns more with the DMN (supporting introspective, memory-guided control) and another aligns with the dorsal attention network (DAN) (supporting world-facing selection), a division replicated and sharpened in recent perturbation and neuromodulation work 6, 34. When problems are perceptually anchored, DAN-FPN coupling implements precise sensory gating and orienting; when they are model-anchored, DMN-FPN coupling integrates stored knowledge and simulation into the control loop-consistent with emerging naturalistic and creative-task data and with reports that DMN subnetworks differentially couple to control and language systems 35, 36, 37.

Energetically, this network is expensive and must be stabilized. Simultaneous PET-fMRI shows that task-positive control responses coincide with heightened glucose metabolism, and whole-brain analyses tie increases in control energy (time-averaged control costs) to oxygen metabolism 38. Large-sample work in 2024 indicates that metabolic costs concentrate in hub regions and rise with task-driven reconfiguration-exactly where frontoparietal and salience hubs sit-offering a physiological reason the system is both potent and fragile under fatigue or pathology 39, 40.

Development and individual variation make the same point from another angle. Mapping individual-specific MD nodes shows pronounced selectivity increases with executive function during development 41, and adolescence is marked by concurrent maturation of aperiodic/E-I signatures and working-memory capacity 42. These changes are what you would expect if the control "OS" is coming online: longer timescales, more selective codes, and more efficient hub reconfiguration.

The network architecture of general intelligence in the human connectome

Why does the MD/FPN so tightly index general intelligence? The core of P-FIT still holds-individual differences in reasoning and "g" emerge from a distributed parieto-frontal system-but the last few years sharpen the picture from where to how. Large-sample and multi-task work shows that people with higher ability more readily occupy a task-optimal MD state shared across diverse paradigms, and the occurrence and stability of this state predict control performance; in other words, smarter brains get to (and stay in) the right control regime with less fuss 44. Converging dynamic-connectivity studies report that higher g is associated with more typical, efficient, and stable macroscale dynamics, and with less unnecessary reconfiguration between rest and multiple task states-consistent with an architecture already closer to task demands 45, 46. At the same time, when problems require internal modeling, high performers exhibit selective FPN-DMN cooperation and flexible switching, a pattern now tied to complex cognition and creative search at scale; what differentiates ability is not chronic anti-correlation but the capacity to engage the right coupling at the right time 32.

Causally, lesions and perturbations keep the arrow pointed at the multiple-demand network rather than perisylvian language cortex 47: focal damage within MD hubs degrades fluid intelligence 48, graph-lesion mapping localizes the deficit to fronto-parietal nodes/edges 49, and neuromodulatory or stimulation manipulations over parietal/dlPFC move reasoning and goal coding 50. White-matter scaffolding matters, too: bridging tracts-especially SLF II/III and long fronto-temporal/parietal pathways-support executive functions, working memory, and flexible control, providing the substrate on which flexible-hub dynamics ride 51. Finally, updates from systems neuroscience elevate the associative thalamus (notably mediodorsal) from relay to regulator: MD thalamus helps stabilize set, resolve uncertainty, and shape prefrontal dynamics, offering a mechanism for set stability under volatility that generalizes across tasks and species 12, 13.

A modern "P-FIT-plus" therefore has three load-bearing parts. (i) Structure: integrity of fronto-parietal nodes and their connecting tracts (e.g., SLF), which provide bandwidth for relational integration. (ii) Dynamics: a flexible-hub operating mode that minimizes gratuitous reconfiguration yet selectively retunes coupling and spectral/timescale properties to meet the problem-including context-dependent FPN-DMN teaming. (iii) Subcortical orchestration: thalamocortical loops (MD<->PFC and partners) that coordinate set control and uncertainty, allowing the system to enter and hold the task-optimal state. Together these features explain why the MD/FPN is the best single neural predictor of complex cognition today: it is the brain’s general-purpose control fabric, and general intelligence reflects how well that fabric is wired, tuned, and coordinated.
